December 2012 ## **26****th** **November– 7****th** **December** # Market turns mildly positive The domestic market has experienced a short-term warm-up in the last two weeks, with both prices and trading volumes up. The spot premium for imported cathode rose by around $10/t to $40-60/t in the two weeks since our last CCF; and premiums for SXEW cathode were also up $5/t to $35-45/t. Domestic cathode prices started picking up at the end of November after falling to a 3 month low in the middle of the month. The SHFE three-month copper price increased to RMB57,150/t on 7th December, up 1.9% from RMB56,090/t at the time of our last publication on 23rd November. SHMET spot market prices rose to RMB 57,025/t on 7th December, up 2.4% from RMB55,700/t on 23rd November. Price pickup in the last 2 weeks

According to a survey by the Shanghai Metals market, operating rates at 20 Chinese wire and cable producers increased to 79.39% in November, up from 75.42% in October, as demand improved and major producers gained some new orders from the State Grid Corporation of China. The latest survey is in line with what we are hearing from market participants. A Chinese trader told us that his customers have © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** **December 2012** www.crugroup.com started ordering cathode stocks from overseas smelters ahead of February’s Chinese New Year holiday, as they believe the spot premium may go higher as activity picks up. Domestic stocks within China also fell over the last two weeks, with stocks on the SHFE (excluding bonded SHFE) falling to 151,901t on 7th December, down 5.8% from 161,306t on 23rd November. This is in accordance with what we have heard from a market source, who said that cathode stocks in several major domestic warehouses in Shanghai have fallen over the last two weeks, as less people are taking cathode from bonded warehouses into the domestic market due to an unfavourable arbitrage for imports. The falling domestic stocks and demand for restocking will support spot prices, but we have to wait and see how long this rebound of spot prices can continue, as demand for cathode from northern China is weakening as temperatures start to plummet and construction slows. However, from our conversations with market participants, we estimate that stocks in Shanghai bonded warehouses reached 750,000-800,000t in early December, up from 700,000—750,000t two weeks ago. We have heard that Chinese smelters have increased their exports to bonded warehouses in No

vember, as they are trying to sell more at the end of the year in order to reach annual targets. More cargoes have also arrived at bonded warehouses in November. Despite some initial signs of pickup in physical demand in China, we believe that Chinese smelters are still getting a better price for stocks that they “export” to the bonded warehouses due to a favourable price gap for exports. The price gap is also suppressing the incentive to take goods from the bonded warehouses to the domestic Chinese market. It is important to note that the cathode stocks in bonded warehouses of Shanghai are unlikely to flow into China in the short run, unless a very profitable price gap (arbitrage room) opens up, or Chinese government puts stricter controls on copper financing in an attempt to tighten the money supply. In our view, both of these eventualities are unlikely, because any favourable arbitrage for importing would be quickly closed by a pickup in the domestic flow of cathode into China, and the Chinese government is not poised to conduct monetary tightening as the economy recovers from a period of weaker growth in Q3. Meanwhile, we have not heard any changes on stocks in bonded warehouses in Guangdong, so total visible stocks in China come to 1,001,901t by 7th December. # Chinese buyers secure a US$12/t premium reduction Codelco reached an agreement with major Chinese buyers last week to settle the annual long-term contract premiums for cathode sales in 2013 at $98/t cif, down $12/t from 2012. Chinese buyers claimed to have suffered big losses in 2012 as they bought from Codelco at a high price of $110/t, whilst spot market premiums have stayed at levels around $50-60/t most of the year. It is worth noting that the yoy decrease for Chinese buyers premium, at 11%, is larger than the 8.6% reduction secured by Codelco’s customers in other Asian countries including Taiwan, Japan and South Korea, and much larger than the 5.6% decrease for its European customers. We think this shows the difficulty Codelco is having in trying to push for higher premiums in the region against a backdrop of normalising growth (as opposed to hyper growth) and a high stocks environment. © 2012 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 5 **December 2012** www.crugroup.com Arbitrage favourable for imports

However, the premium of $98/t is still considered to be higher than the market’s previous expectation of $95/t; we believe this is because some new comers to the market are trying to grab a bigger market share by engaging in long-term contracts with Codelco. We have also confirmed that Codelco cut its contract volumes t

o China in 2013, predominantly due to maintenance work to be carried out at its Chuquicamata smelter. Our conversations with major traders suggest that the volumes might fall by 10-20% from 2012’s level; with one source suggesting annual contract volumes in China could be down by as much as a quarter or 80,000t (out of 320,000t). We believe the relatively high premium might make it difficult for other suppliers of refined copper to settle long term agreements. Therefore, we expect the majority of Chinese buyers will sign less contracted volume in 2013, and due to the high base of imports in 2012, we also expect to see a y- o-y decrease in China’s cathode imports in 2013. This may give some support to spot premiums in China next year. A source at a trading branch of a major smelter has confirmed that they will sign less contracted volumes and buy more from the spot market in 2013 as the costs are expected to be much lower than taking the annual premium. **Data: CRU Analysis** # China may resume VAT rebate on some semis exports There were media reports earlier this week suggesting that the Chinese government may reinstate previously expired (July 15 2010) VAT rebates for the exports of various products from January 2013 in a move to boost exports. These include fertilisers, steel and nonferrous metals products including some copper semis. The government made the move in 2010 to control the expansion of capacity in low-valueadded products. There have been some suggestions that the governmwent may also lower export taxes for some products at the same time. We noted the possibility of such policies in our 9th November CCF, however, we expect the reinstating of rebates to have a limited impact on semis exports, as the products involved only amount to around 10,000 t/m and are mainly low-end and manufactured by small-sized producers. We believe this move is targeted to support smaller Chinese semis producers who have © 2012 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 5 **December 2012** www.crugroup.com struggled this year as operating rates have remained below 2011 levels for most of the year. We expect some other targeted measures could also be announced for specific sectors, such as another round of rebates for autos and white goods, however, these would not represent a significant economic stimulus. # A modest improvement in the data outlook A recent news article suggested that the latest Chinese copper data h

eld a “warning signal,” and that rising stock levels in Shanghai, combined with import numbers for October, indicated “a month-on-month drop of almost 20% in Chinese apparent copper demand.” 

While we acknowledge that the Chinese economy went through a soft patch in Q3 of 2012, and last week in the copper monitor we commented on the dampened consumption of copper tube, we are far less inclined to believe that these data points are signs of a rapid contraction in Chinese copper consumption for several reasons. 

As we highlighted in our last CCF, October’s imports in 2011 were atypical in that they actually rose from September, an occurrence driven by large price movements in October 2011, that typically should not occur given that  ports in China are closed for a quarter of the month for a national holiday. Therefore, the October 2012 import headlines are heavily distorted by seasonal effects and base effects from 2011. Secondly, looking at the range of Chinese economic indicators that CRU’s economics team regularly monitor, we saw a modest uptick in October activity, and this is a trend we expect to continue through Q4.  The growth in the three month moving average of fixed asset investment accelerated to 21.5% y-o-y, from 20.8% y-o-y in the previous period; with the largest upswing in investment occurring in the area of infrastructure, a positive for copper demand.  China’s industrial production also showed a moderate annual increase in the month, along with an index of leading indicators from China’s statistics bureau.  At an end-use level, the production of air conditioners was up 31.2% y-o-y in October following heavy y-o-y declines in Q3.  Whilst this data is only a snapshot for October, more positive news has since emerged in with November’s HSBC/Markit PMI hitting 50.5, the highest reading in 13 months. 

Finally, after a period of softer production from Chinese physical copper consumers in the third quarter, we expect their production output to rebound in the final quarter as companies increase production to meet annual targets.  From speaking to a source at a large Chinese smelter, we have heard that their downstream customers who produce copper rod have increased their orders in November, and have started rebuilding stocks after holding lower stocks in Q3. 

Whilst the raw numbers may make for an excellent headline, digging a little deeper reveals a far less gloomy outlook for copper consumption in China.
